problem: The chapter says a quarter-wave plate makes plane polarized light circularly polarized without any condition on the orientation of the incident plane. This is false in general: circular polarization needs the two components to have equal amplitude, which happens only when the incident plane is at 45° to the optic axis. At any other angle the output is elliptically polarized, so a student will write the unconditional statement in the exam and lose marks.
fix: A quarter-wave plate introduces a path difference of λ/4 (phase difference π/2) between its two components. When the incident plane of polarization is at 45° to the optic axis, the two components have equal amplitude and the emergent light is circularly polarized; at other angles the emergent light is elliptically polarized.

problem: "a number between 0 and 1 gives the fraction that is polarized" is loose. The standard quantity is the degree of polarization, defined from the maximum and minimum intensities seen as the analyser turns, not simply a fraction of the intensity.
fix: Partially polarized light is a mixture of polarized and unpolarized light. Its degree of polarization is P = (I_max − I_min)/(I_max + I_min), where I_max and I_min are the largest and smallest intensities transmitted as the analyser is rotated; P = 0 is unpolarized light and P = 1 is plane polarized light.

problem: "do not add 90° to the incidence angle" is ambiguous — a student cannot tell whether 90° is being added to θ_p or subtracted to get the refraction angle.
fix: At Brewster's angle θ_p + θ_r = 90°, where θ_r is the angle of refraction; so θ_r = 90° − θ_p (33.7° for glass), not θ_p + 90°.

problem: The answer states the 90° separation as the cause of full polarization without the physical link. The 90° separation and the full polarization both follow from Brewster's condition; the reason the in-plane component vanishes is that the dipoles in the medium oscillate along the refracted ray's direction and cannot radiate along that same direction.
fix: 90°, because at Brewster's angle θ_p + θ_r = 90°. The dipoles in the medium oscillate along the direction of the refracted ray's in-plane component, which then points along the reflected ray; a dipole cannot radiate along its own axis, so the in-plane component is missing from the reflected beam and only the perpendicular component remains.
